osces.title: Acute Suicidal Ideation - Risk Assessment and Mental Health Act
osces.clinical_scenario: Sarah Chen, a 28-year-old graphic designer, presents to the emergency department at 2 AM accompanied by her partner. She has been experiencing severe depression for 3 months following a job loss and relationship breakdown. Tonight she wrote a suicide note and was found by her partner searching online for 'painless ways to die'. She has 100 paracetamol tablets at home and lives on the 15th floor of an apartment building. Her partner reports she has been drinking heavily (bottle of wine daily) for the past month. Sarah states 'I just want the pain to stop' and admits to planning to take all the tablets after her partner fell asleep.

patient_demographics.name: Sarah Chen
patient_demographics.medical_history: Depression diagnosed 2 years ago, one previous overdose attempt age 23 (10 paracetamol tablets), generalised anxiety disorder
patient_demographics.medications: Sertraline 50mg daily (PBS code: 8182K) - stopped 6 weeks ago, previously on desvenlafaxine 100mg daily
patient_demographics.social_history: Lives with partner in high-rise apartment, no children, parents live interstate, lost job 3 months ago, drinking 1 bottle wine/day, no illicit drugs, 5 cigarettes/day
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother has bipolar disorder, maternal aunt died by suicide age 45, father has alcohol use disorder

tasks.task: Perform a comprehensive suicide risk assessment using the SAFE-T framework
marking_criteria: Establishes rapport with empathetic, non-judgemental approach
Assesses specific plan: method (paracetamol overdose), access (100 tablets at home), timing (tonight after partner asleep)
Evaluates lethality of plan and access to other means (height - 15th floor)
Explores precipitating factors: job loss, relationship issues, alcohol use
Assesses protective factors: partner support, help-seeking behaviour, future orientation
Reviews previous attempts: details of prior overdose, medical treatment received, triggers
Screens for hopelessness using direct questions about future
Evaluates substance use impact: alcohol disinhibition, impaired judgement
Assesses current mental state: mood, affect, psychotic symptoms, insight
Determines immediate risk level as HIGH requiring admission
Documents using Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale or similar tool

tasks.task: Explain the Mental Health Act assessment and involuntary admission process
marking_criteria: Clearly explains Schedule 1 criteria under NSW Mental Health Act 2007
States patient has mental illness (major depression) affecting judgement
Identifies immediate risk of serious harm to self
Explains no less restrictive alternative available given high risk
Discusses patient's right to refuse voluntary admission
Outlines medical certificate process valid for 24 hours
Explains transport to mental health unit via ambulance or police if needed
Describes psychiatrist review required within 12 hours of admission
Mentions patient rights: legal representation, tribunal review, appeals process
Provides information about support person/advocate involvement
Addresses patient concerns with empathy while maintaining safety focus

tasks.task: Develop an immediate safety plan and initial management
marking_criteria: Arranges immediate psychiatric review in emergency department
Implements environmental safety: remove means, constant observation
Contacts mental health crisis team for admission coordination
Involves partner in safety planning with patient consent
Prescribes appropriate medication: lorazepam 1-2mg PO/SL PRN (PBS code: 2195Y)
Orders baseline investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, BSL, BAL, urine drug screen
Documents comprehensive risk assessment in medical record
Arranges removal of means from home: partner to secure medications, consider temporary relocation
Provides crisis helpline numbers: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636
Plans follow-up: psychiatry review within 24 hours, psychology referral, case management
Addresses alcohol withdrawal risk: thiamine 300mg IV, CIWA-Ar monitoring

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: dishevelled, poor eye contact, tearful. Behaviour: psychomotor retardation, cooperative. Speech: soft, slow, normal articulation. Mood: 'hopeless'. Affect: depressed, restricted range, mood congruent. Thought form: linear, goal-directed. Thought content: suicidal ideation with plan, themes of worthlessness, guilt about being a burden. Perceptions: denies hallucinations. Cognition: alert, oriented, concentrating poorly. Insight: partial - acknowledges depression but minimises risk. Judgement: impaired by depression
expected_findings.risk_assessment: HIGH ACUTE RISK - Current suicidal ideation with specific plan (paracetamol overdose), access to means (100 tablets), intent expressed, previous attempt, current depression with hopelessness, alcohol use increasing impulsivity, limited protective factors. Requires immediate psychiatric admission under Mental Health Act
expected_findings.management_priorities: 1. Ensure immediate safety - constant observation, 2. Mental Health Act assessment for involuntary admission, 3. Remove access to means, 4. Treat depression and alcohol use, 5. Engage support network, 6. Intensive follow-up post-discharge

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient initially minimises risk but gradually reveals plan details. Shows ambivalence about dying - wants pain to stop but scared of death. Becomes tearful when discussing partner's support. If candidate is empathetic, provides more information. If confrontational, becomes guarded. Tests candidate's ability to balance therapeutic rapport with safety requirements under Mental Health Act.
common_pitfalls: Failing to ask directly about suicide plan details and access to means
Not recognising HIGH risk requiring immediate admission
Inadequate knowledge of Mental Health Act criteria and process
Missing alcohol withdrawal risk in management plan
Not involving partner/support network in safety planning
Forgetting to remove access to means from home environment

osces.title: First Episode Psychosis - Early Intervention and Antipsychotic Initiation
osces.clinical_scenario: James Thompson, a 19-year-old university student, is brought to the emergency department by campus security after being found on the roof of his dormitory at 3 AM claiming he could fly. His roommate reports that over the past 3 weeks, James has been staying up all night writing 'mathematical proofs that prove God speaks through prime numbers'. He believes his professor has implanted a microchip in his brain to steal his revolutionary theories. He has been posting bizarre content on social media about government surveillance through WiFi signals. Cannabis use is suspected. His academic performance has declined sharply from distinction average to failing. No prior psychiatric history.

patient_demographics.name: James Thompson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Bizarre behaviour and beliefs for 3 weeks
patient_demographics.medical_history: No significant medical history, no prior psychiatric contact, mild asthma
patient_demographics.medications: Salbutamol inhaler PRN (PBS code: 1234R), no regular medications
patient_demographics.social_history: Lives on campus, single, parents live rurally 300km away, high achiever academically until recently, admits to cannabis use 'occasionally', denies other drugs, minimal alcohol, non-smoker
patient_demographics.family_history: Paternal uncle has schizophrenia, mother has anxiety disorder, no other significant history

tasks.task: Conduct a comprehensive assessment for first episode psychosis
marking_criteria: Establishes rapport using non-confrontational approach
Explores onset and progression: acute (3 weeks) vs insidious
Identifies positive symptoms: delusions (grandiose, paranoid), thought broadcasting
Screens for hallucinations: auditory, visual, tactile, olfactory
Assesses negative symptoms: social withdrawal, avolition, affective flattening
Evaluates cognitive symptoms: attention, executive function, memory
Explores functional impact: academic decline, self-care, social relationships
Screens for mood symptoms: mania, depression (psychotic depression vs schizophrenia)
Takes detailed substance use history: cannabis frequency, potency, other drugs
Assesses risk: suicide (10% lifetime risk in schizophrenia), violence, vulnerability
Considers differential diagnoses: substance-induced, mania with psychosis, brief psychotic disorder
Documents Duration of Untreated Psychosis (DUP) - critical for prognosis

tasks.task: Explain diagnosis and treatment plan to patient and family
marking_criteria: Uses appropriate language avoiding jargon
Explains first episode psychosis as treatable condition with good prognosis if treated early
Discusses role of stress-vulnerability model
Addresses cannabis as potential trigger requiring cessation
Outlines need for antipsychotic medication to treat symptoms
Explains admission to youth mental health unit for safety and assessment
Describes multidisciplinary team approach: psychiatry, psychology, social work
Discusses typical treatment duration: minimum 12 months after remission
Mentions early intervention service referral for age-appropriate care
Provides realistic prognosis: 80% significant improvement with treatment
Addresses family concerns and provides psychoeducation resources

tasks.task: Initiate appropriate antipsychotic treatment and monitoring
marking_criteria: Chooses appropriate first-line antipsychotic: aripiprazole 10mg daily (PBS code: 8532M)
Explains lower starting dose for first episode (aripiprazole 5-10mg vs 15-30mg)
Orders baseline investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT, lipids, HbA1c, prolactin, ECG
Arranges urine drug screen and considers CT/MRI brain
Prescribes benzodiazepine for acute agitation: lorazepam 1mg PO/IM PRN (PBS code: 2195Y)
Explains common side effects: sedation, weight gain, metabolic effects
Discusses rare but serious: NMS, tardive dyskinesia, QT prolongation
Plans regular monitoring: weight, waist circumference, BP, glucose, lipids
Addresses adherence strategies: psychoeducation, family involvement, long-acting injectable option
Arranges follow-up: weekly initially, therapeutic drug monitoring if required
Documents informed consent including right to refuse treatment

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: dishevelled, suspicious gaze, wearing multiple layers. Behaviour: guarded, scanning room, mild psychomotor agitation. Speech: normal rate and volume, circumstantial. Mood: 'revolutionary'. Affect: labile, inappropriate smile. Thought form: tangential, loose associations. Thought content: grandiose delusions (mathematical genius), paranoid delusions (microchip), ideas of reference (WiFi surveillance). Perceptions: denies hallucinations currently. Cognition: oriented, attention impaired. Insight: absent - no awareness of illness. Judgement: severely impaired
expected_findings.investigations: Urine drug screen: THC positive. FBC, UEC, LFT, TSH: normal. Lipids: normal baseline. HbA1c: 5.2%. ECG: normal QTc 420ms. CT brain: normal. Prolactin: 15 ng/mL (normal)
expected_findings.diagnosis: First episode psychosis, likely schizophreniform disorder vs substance-induced psychotic disorder (cannabis). Duration 3 weeks (requires 1 month for schizophreniform, 6 months for schizophrenia)

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient exhibits paranoid behaviour initially but engages if approached calmly. Demonstrates tangential thinking and incorporates mathematical concepts inappropriately. May become suspicious of examiner being part of surveillance. Tests candidate's ability to assess psychosis while maintaining therapeutic rapport. Family member (if introduced) is worried but supportive.
common_pitfalls: Confronting delusions directly rather than exploring phenomenology
Missing substance use history or minimising cannabis role
Starting antipsychotic at standard rather than first-episode dose
Not involving family/carers in treatment planning
Forgetting baseline metabolic monitoring before antipsychotics
Missing risk assessment particularly vulnerability and self-neglect

osces.title: Major Depressive Disorder - SSRI Selection and Monitoring
osces.clinical_scenario: Margaret Wilson, a 42-year-old primary school teacher, presents to her GP with a 4-month history of persistent low mood, crying spells at work, and difficulty getting out of bed. She reports losing interest in teaching, which she previously loved, and has taken 15 sick days this term. She wakes at 4 AM most mornings and cannot return to sleep, spending hours ruminating about perceived failures. She has lost 8kg unintentionally and her husband reports she barely touches her dinner. Her concentration is so poor she cannot read or follow TV programs. She scores 19 on PHQ-9 (moderately severe depression). She states 'I feel like a burden to everyone' but denies active suicidal ideation.

patient_demographics.name: Margaret Wilson
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Low mood, anhedonia, and functional decline for 4 months
patient_demographics.medical_history: Hypothyroidism (controlled), IBS, one episode postnatal depression 10 years ago treated with counselling only
patient_demographics.social_history: Married 15 years, two children (10 and 12), supportive husband, no alcohol or substance use, never smoked, regular exercise until 4 months ago
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother had recurrent depression, father has anxiety disorder, no bipolar disorder or suicide

tasks.task: Assess depression severity and determine treatment approach
marking_criteria: Uses validated tool: PHQ-9 score 19 indicates moderately severe depression
Explores all DSM-5 criteria systematically: mood, anhedonia, weight loss, insomnia, psychomotor changes, fatigue, worthlessness, concentration, suicidal ideation
Identifies melancholic features: early morning wakening, mood worse in morning, marked anhedonia, excessive guilt
Screens for bipolar disorder: past hypomanic/manic episodes
Assesses functional impact: work performance, relationships, self-care
Explores psychosocial stressors: work stress, relationship issues, financial concerns
Reviews previous episode: postnatal depression severity, treatment response
Screens for anxiety disorders: GAD-7 or similar tool
Orders investigations to exclude organic causes: FBC, UEC, TSH, B12, folate, vitamin D
Assesses suicide risk: passive ideation only, no plan or intent
Determines severity as moderate-severe requiring medication plus therapy

tasks.task: Select and prescribe appropriate SSRI with patient education
marking_criteria: Selects appropriate first-line SSRI: escitalopram 10mg daily (PBS code: 8785H)
Explains rationale: efficacy, tolerability, minimal drug interactions
Discusses alternative options: sertraline 50mg (PBS code: 8182K) if cost concern
Educates about delayed onset: 2-4 weeks for initial response, 6-8 weeks for full effect
Reviews common side effects: initial nausea, headache, anxiety, sexual dysfunction
Warns about initial activation/anxiety and potential suicidal ideation increase
Explains not addictive but discusses discontinuation syndrome
Advises continuing 6-12 months after remission to prevent relapse
Discusses dose titration: start 10mg, may increase to 20mg after 4 weeks
Provides written information and reputable resources (Beyond Blue, Black Dog Institute)
Arranges safety net: review in 1-2 weeks, earlier if deterioration

tasks.task: Develop comprehensive management plan including non-pharmacological interventions
marking_criteria: Refers for psychological therapy: CBT or IPT via Mental Health Treatment Plan
Explains Medicare rebates: 6 initial + 4 additional sessions per calendar year
Recommends structured behavioural activation: activity scheduling, pleasant events
Addresses sleep hygiene: regular schedule, avoid screens, relaxation techniques
Encourages gradual return to exercise: start with 10-minute walks
Discusses work modifications: reduced hours initially, stress management
Involves support network: husband education, family therapy if needed
Provides crisis resources: Lifeline 13 11 14, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636
Addresses nutrition: regular meals despite poor appetite
Plans monitoring: PHQ-9 at each visit, side effect assessment
Discusses prognosis: 60-70% respond to first SSRI, options if non-response
Documents Mental Health Treatment Plan for Medicare rebates

expected_findings.investigations: TSH: 2.1 mIU/L (normal on treatment), FBC: normal, B12: 180 pmol/L (low-normal), folate: 18 nmol/L (normal), vitamin D: 45 nmol/L (insufficient), ferritin: 30 μg/L (low-normal)
expected_findings.diagnosis: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate to severe, with melancholic features. PHQ-9 score 19/27
expected_findings.prognosis: Good prognostic factors: first episode in 10 years, supportive family, help-seeking, no substance use, previous good function. Risk factors: family history, melancholic features

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient is cooperative but speaks slowly with psychomotor retardation. Becomes tearful when discussing impact on family. Shows good insight and motivation for treatment but worried about medication side effects and stigma. Tests candidate's ability to select appropriate SSRI and provide comprehensive depression management.
common_pitfalls: Not using validated assessment tool (PHQ-9 or DASS)
Missing melancholic features which may influence treatment choice
Forgetting to screen for bipolar disorder before starting SSRI
Not addressing common SSRI concerns (addiction, personality change)
Inadequate safety netting for early SSRI activation
Forgetting Mental Health Treatment Plan for psychology rebates

osces.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder - CBT vs Medication
osces.clinical_scenario: David Kim, a 35-year-old accountant, presents with 8 months of excessive worry about multiple life domains. He worries constantly about work performance despite excellent reviews, his children's safety despite no threats, and finances despite stable income. He experiences muscle tension requiring weekly massages, feels 'on edge' constantly, and has difficulty falling asleep due to racing thoughts. His wife reports he seeks constant reassurance and avoids making decisions. He scores 16 on GAD-7 (severe anxiety). His anxiety worsened after a colleague's sudden death from heart attack. He drinks 6 cups of coffee daily to combat fatigue from poor sleep.

patient_demographics.name: David Kim
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Constant worry and anxiety for 8 months
patient_demographics.medical_history: Irritable bowel syndrome, tension headaches, no prior psychiatric history
patient_demographics.medications: Hyoscine butylbromide PRN for IBS (PBS code: 1234H), paracetamol PRN
patient_demographics.social_history: Married 8 years, two children aged 4 and 6, mortgage stress, works 50+ hours/week, 6 coffees/day, social drinker (2-3 standard drinks weekly), never smoked, stopped exercise due to time pressure
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother has GAD on medication, sister has panic disorder, no bipolar or psychosis

tasks.task: Comprehensive anxiety assessment and diagnosis
marking_criteria: Uses GAD-7 systematically: score 16 indicates severe anxiety
Explores all GAD criteria: excessive worry, difficulty controlling worry, 6+ months duration
Identifies associated symptoms: restlessness, fatigue, concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance
Screens for other anxiety disorders: panic disorder, social anxiety, specific phobias, OCD
Assesses for depression: PHQ-9 or similar mood screening
Explores functional impact: work performance anxiety, relationship strain, avoidance
Identifies maintaining factors: excessive caffeine, reassurance seeking, avoidance
Reviews physical symptoms: IBS, headaches, muscle tension as anxiety manifestations
Considers medical differentials: thyroid, cardiac, caffeine excess
Explores specific worry themes: work, family, health, finances
Assesses insight and motivation for change

tasks.task: Discuss treatment options comparing CBT and medication
marking_criteria: Explains CBT principles: identifying and challenging worry thoughts, behavioural experiments
Describes CBT techniques: worry time, problem-solving, relaxation training
States CBT efficacy: 50-60% response rate, effects maintained long-term
Explains medication options: SSRI/SNRI first line for GAD
Recommends specific medication: escitalopram 10mg (PBS code: 8785H) or duloxetine 30mg (PBS code: 8826K)
Compares onset: CBT gradual over 8-12 weeks, medication 4-6 weeks
Discusses combination therapy: CBT + medication superior to either alone
Reviews side effects: medication (nausea, sexual dysfunction) vs CBT (initial anxiety increase)
Considers patient preference: time commitment, cost, stigma concerns
Explains Medicare rebates: Mental Health Treatment Plan for psychology
Recommends stepped care: mild-moderate CBT first, severe consider combination
Addresses maintenance: CBT skills permanent, medication may need 12+ months

tasks.task: Develop anxiety management plan with lifestyle modifications
marking_criteria: Addresses caffeine reduction: maximum 2-3 cups/day, none after 2 PM
Implements sleep hygiene: consistent bedtime, wind-down routine, bedroom environment
Introduces relaxation techniques: progressive muscle relaxation, breathing exercises
Recommends exercise: 30 minutes moderate exercise 5 days/week for anxiety reduction
Suggests mindfulness: apps (Smiling Mind, Headspace), MBSR programs
Plans worry time: scheduled 15 minutes daily for worry, postpone worries outside this
Reduces reassurance seeking: involve wife in not providing excessive reassurance
Addresses work-life balance: boundary setting, delegation, realistic expectations
Provides resources: Beyond Blue, MindSpot online CBT, Anxiety Australia
Arranges follow-up: 2 weeks to assess response, earlier if deterioration
Documents care plan with specific goals and timeframes

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: well-groomed, fidgety. Behaviour: cooperative but restless, foot tapping. Speech: normal rate, occasionally circumstantial. Mood: 'stressed'. Affect: anxious, appropriate. Thought form: goal-directed but preoccupied with worries. Thought content: no psychosis, catastrophic thinking patterns. Perceptions: nil abnormal. Cognition: alert, mild concentration impairment. Insight: good - recognises excessive worry. Judgement: intact
expected_findings.diagnosis: Generalized Anxiety Disorder, severe (GAD-7 score 16/21). Secondary IBS and tension headaches. Caffeine use disorder contributing
expected_findings.investigations: TSH, FBC, UEC to exclude medical causes. ECG if palpitations. Consider sleep study if snoring/apnoea suspected

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient is articulate but seeks reassurance repeatedly during consultation. Asks multiple 'what if' questions. Shows physical signs of anxiety (fidgeting, muscle tension). Interested in treatment but concerned about time for therapy and medication side effects. Wife may attend - frustrated by constant reassurance seeking.
common_pitfalls: Not using structured assessment tool (GAD-7)
Missing excessive caffeine as perpetuating factor
Not explaining differences between CBT and medication adequately
Forgetting to address reassurance seeking behaviour
Not considering combination therapy for severe anxiety
Missing functional impact on work and relationships

osces.title: Bipolar Disorder Manic Episode - Mood Stabilizer Initiation
osces.clinical_scenario: Rebecca Martinez, a 26-year-old marketing manager, is brought to emergency by police after being found at 4 AM trying to purchase a $80,000 sports car with her credit card. She has slept 2 hours per night for the past week, believing sleep is 'for mortals'. She reports feeling 'absolutely incredible' and has been working on a 'revolutionary marketing campaign that will change humanity'. She sent 200 emails to the CEO last night with 'breakthrough ideas'. Her partner reports she spent $15,000 on online shopping in 3 days, is talking rapidly about starting five new businesses simultaneously, and had unprotected sex with strangers twice this week, which is completely out of character. She has pressured speech and becomes irritable when interrupted.

patient_demographics.name: Rebecca Martinez
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Elevated mood and decreased sleep for 1 week
patient_demographics.medical_history: Two previous depressive episodes age 22 and 24, treated with sertraline, PCOS
patient_demographics.medications: Metformin 500mg BD for PCOS (PBS code: 3456M), ceased sertraline 3 months ago
patient_demographics.social_history: Lives with partner of 3 years, no children but trying to conceive, social drinker, tried cocaine once at university, non-smoker, usually exercises regularly
patient_demographics.family_history: Father has bipolar disorder type I, paternal grandmother died by suicide during depression, mother has anxiety

tasks.task: Assess manic episode and establish bipolar diagnosis
marking_criteria: Identifies current manic symptoms: elevated mood, decreased sleep, grandiosity, increased activity
Assesses additional symptoms: pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, poor judgement
Determines episode duration: >7 days meets mania criteria (vs hypomania <7 days)
Evaluates functional impact: work inappropriate behaviour, financial losses, relationship risk
Reviews previous episodes: two depressions suggest bipolar II becoming bipolar I
Screens for psychotic features: grandiose delusions about changing humanity
Assesses risk: financial ruin, sexual health risks, vulnerability to exploitation
Explores triggers: antidepressant discontinuation, stress, sleep deprivation
Uses Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) for severity: likely >20 (moderate-severe)
Considers differentials: substance-induced, hyperthyroidism, brain lesion
Documents criteria for involuntary admission if refuses treatment

tasks.task: Initiate mood stabilizer treatment with appropriate monitoring
marking_criteria: Selects appropriate mood stabilizer: lithium carbonate 450mg nocte (PBS code: 1245L)
Explains lithium as gold standard for bipolar with anti-suicide properties
Discusses alternatives if planning pregnancy: sodium valproate contraindicated
Orders baseline tests: UEC, TFT, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test, weight
Explains therapeutic range: 0.6-0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, 0.8-1.0 for acute
Describes monitoring: levels at 5 days, then weekly until stable
Reviews common side effects: tremor, polyuria, polydipsia, weight gain, nausea
Warns about toxicity: confusion, ataxia, severe tremor >1.5 mmol/L
Advises hydration importance and avoiding NSAIDs
Prescribes acute management: olanzapine 10mg nocte (PBS code: 8532M) for rapid control
Plans contraception discussion given teratogenicity risks
Documents informed consent and provides lithium information sheet

tasks.task: Develop comprehensive management plan and psychoeducation
marking_criteria: Arranges admission to psychiatric unit for safety and stabilisation
Implements financial protection: involve partner, limit credit card access
Addresses sexual health: STI screening, emergency contraception if needed
Plans sleep restoration: sleep hygiene, short-term sedation
Refers to bipolar disorder specialist/clinic for ongoing management
Recommends mood charting: daily mood, sleep, medication tracking
Discusses long-term prophylaxis: lithium reduces relapse by 30-40%
Explains bipolar disorder: chronic condition requiring lifelong management
Provides psychoeducation resources: SANE Australia, Black Dog Institute bipolar guides
Plans psychological intervention: IPSRT or CBT for bipolar when stable
Addresses work: medical certificate, gradual return when euthymic
Involves partner: education about early warning signs, support strategies

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: bright clothing, excessive makeup, dishevelled. Behaviour: hyperactive, intrusive, difficulty sitting still. Speech: pressured, loud, difficult to interrupt. Mood: 'fantastic, best ever'. Affect: euphoric, labile, irritable when challenged. Thought form: flight of ideas, circumstantial. Thought content: grandiose ideas, poor judgement, no insight. Perceptions: denies hallucinations. Cognition: alert, distractible, poor concentration. Insight: absent - no awareness of illness. Judgement: severely impaired
expected_findings.investigations: Pregnancy test: negative. UEC: normal, eGFR >90. TFT: TSH 2.0 (normal). ECG: sinus tachycardia 110bpm. FBC: normal. Calcium: 2.35 mmol/L. Urine drug screen: negative
expected_findings.diagnosis: Bipolar Affective Disorder Type I, current episode manic without psychotic features. Previous depressive episodes likely bipolar depression misdiagnosed as MDD

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient is euphoric, talks rapidly, and jumps between topics. Becomes irritable if examiner suggests she is unwell. Makes inappropriate comments about examiner's appearance. Unable to sit still. Partner (if present) is exhausted and frightened. Tests candidate's ability to assess mania while managing challenging behaviour.
common_pitfalls: Not recognising bipolar disorder from history of depression + current mania
Missing pregnancy test before mood stabilizer initiation
Forgetting baseline investigations before lithium
Not addressing immediate risks (financial, sexual health)
Inadequate psychoeducation about chronic nature of bipolar
Using valproate in woman of childbearing age without contraception discussion

osces.title: Alcohol Withdrawal - CIWA-Ar Protocol and Benzodiazepine Dosing
osces.clinical_scenario: Michael O'Brien, a 48-year-old construction worker, presents to emergency 18 hours after his last drink. He has been drinking 1.5 bottles of wine plus 6 beers daily for 5 years, increased from social drinking after a workplace accident. He tried to stop drinking yesterday after his wife threatened to leave. He now has marked tremor, sweating, and nausea. He reports 'feeling bugs crawling on my skin' and is increasingly agitated. His blood pressure is 165/95, pulse 115, and he appears anxious and diaphoretic. He had a witnessed seizure 5 years ago during previous withdrawal attempt. He scores 22 on CIWA-Ar assessment.

patient_demographics.name: Michael O'Brien
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms 18 hours after last drink
patient_demographics.medical_history: Chronic back pain from workplace injury, hepatic steatosis on ultrasound, hypertension, previous withdrawal seizure, gastro-oesophageal reflux
patient_demographics.medications: Tapentadol 100mg BD (PBS code: 5678T), perindopril 5mg daily (PBS code: 8901P), omeprazole 20mg daily (PBS code: 1567O)
patient_demographics.social_history: Married 20 years but relationship strained, 3 teenage children, drinks 18-20 standard drinks daily, 20 cigarettes/day, no illicit drugs, stopped working 2 years ago due to injury
patient_demographics.family_history: Father died from alcoholic liver disease age 62, brother has alcohol use disorder, mother has depression

tasks.task: Perform CIWA-Ar assessment and risk stratification
marking_criteria: Systematically scores all 10 CIWA-Ar items: nausea, tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, tactile, auditory, visual, headache, orientation
Calculates total score: 22 indicates severe withdrawal requiring admission
Identifies high-risk features: previous seizure, score >15, co-morbidities
Assesses for complications: hallucinations (tactile present), seizure risk, delirium tremens risk
Reviews drinking pattern: quantity (18-20 standard drinks), duration (5 years), last drink time
Screens for other substance use: benzodiazepines, opioids (on tapentadol)
Evaluates medical complications: liver disease, electrolyte disturbance, Wernicke's
Documents vital signs: hypertension, tachycardia as withdrawal signs
Assesses motivation for abstinence vs controlled drinking
Determines setting: requires inpatient withdrawal due to severity and seizure history
Plans monitoring frequency: hourly CIWA-Ar initially given severity

tasks.task: Prescribe appropriate benzodiazepine regimen using CIWA-Ar protocol
marking_criteria: Prescribes loading dose: diazepam 20mg PO stat (CIWA-Ar >20) (PBS code: 2622H)
Orders symptom-triggered regimen: CIWA-Ar score 8-14: diazepam 5-10mg, score 15-20: 10-15mg, score >20: 15-20mg
Specifies monitoring: CIWA-Ar hourly for first 8 hours, then 2-hourly
Sets maximum daily dose: usually 60mg/24 hours unless severe
Prescribes thiamine prophylaxis: 300mg IV daily x3 days before glucose (PBS code: 1234T)
Orders supportive medications: metoclopramide 10mg PRN (PBS code: 3456M), paracetamol 1g QID
Addresses seizure risk: considers phenytoin prophylaxis given history
Plans taper: reduce by 10-20% daily once stable for 24 hours
Documents contraindications check: respiratory disease, sleep apnoea
Reviews drug interactions: caution with tapentadol (CNS depression)
Provides PRN parameters: clear instructions for nursing staff
Arranges close monitoring: continuous pulse oximetry initially

tasks.task: Develop comprehensive alcohol treatment plan
marking_criteria: Orders investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT, coagulation, phosphate, magnesium, glucose
Screens for complications: hepatitis serology, ammonia if encephalopathy suspected
Prescribes vitamin supplementation: thiamine, folate, multivitamin
Addresses nutritional needs: dietitian review, regular meals
Discusses anti-craving medications: naltrexone 50mg daily (PBS code: 8734N) or acamprosate 333mg TDS (PBS code: 8756A)
Refers to addiction medicine: specialised assessment and management
Arranges psychological intervention: CBT, motivational interviewing
Provides support services: AA contact, SMART Recovery groups
Involves family: education, Al-Anon support groups
Plans discharge: outpatient follow-up, GP management, relapse prevention
Addresses chronic pain: non-pharmacological strategies, avoid addiction transfer
Documents long-term plan: abstinence goal, harm minimisation if needed

expected_findings.physical_examination: Tremor: coarse, bilateral upper limb. Vital signs: BP 165/95, HR 115, RR 20, afebrile. Diaphoretic, anxious appearance. Tactile hallucinations reported. No asterixis. Abdomen: mild hepatomegaly
expected_findings.investigations: GGT: 180 U/L (elevated), AST: 95 U/L, ALT: 78 U/L, MCV: 102 fL (macrocytosis), albumin: 32 g/L (low), INR: 1.3, phosphate: 0.6 mmol/L (low), magnesium: 0.65 mmol/L (low)
expected_findings.ciwa_scoring: Nausea: 4, Tremor: 5, Sweating: 4, Anxiety: 5, Agitation: 3, Tactile: 1, Auditory: 0, Visual: 0, Headache: 0, Orientation: 0. Total: 22 (severe withdrawal)

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient demonstrates visible tremor and appears sweaty. Becomes increasingly agitated if medication delayed. Reports tactile hallucinations intermittently. Wife (if present) is frustrated but concerned. Tests candidate's systematic CIWA-Ar assessment and benzodiazepine dosing competence.
common_pitfalls: Not calculating CIWA-Ar score systematically
Under-dosing benzodiazepines in severe withdrawal
Forgetting thiamine BEFORE glucose (precipitates Wernicke's)
Missing previous seizure history requiring prophylaxis consideration
Not addressing electrolyte abnormalities (phosphate, magnesium)
Inadequate monitoring frequency in severe withdrawal

osces.title: Delirium - Hypoactive vs Hyperactive Differentiation
osces.clinical_scenario: Dorothy Chang, an 82-year-old retired librarian, was admitted 3 days ago with community-acquired pneumonia. The nursing staff report she has become 'confused' over the past 24 hours. During the day she appears drowsy and withdrawn, staring blankly and not responding to questions. Last night she was trying to climb out of bed, pulling at her IV line, and shouting about 'needing to catch the train to work'. She did not recognise her daughter this morning. Her daughter reports she was cognitively intact before this admission, managing all her own affairs independently. She scores 18/30 on MMSE with poor attention and disorientation to time and place.

patient_demographics.name: Dorothy Chang
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Acute confusion on background of pneumonia treatment
patient_demographics.medical_history: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis, mild hearing impairment, cataract surgery 2022
patient_demographics.medications: Telmisartan 40mg daily (PBS code: 2341T), metformin 500mg BD (PBS code: 3456M), paracetamol 1g QID, currently on ceftriaxone IV for pneumonia
patient_demographics.social_history: Widowed 5 years, lives independently in own home, daughter visits daily, no alcohol, never smoked, walks with single-point stick, active in book club
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother had 'senility' in her 90s, no other psychiatric history

tasks.task: Assess and diagnose delirium with subtype classification
marking_criteria: Uses CAM (Confusion Assessment Method): acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, disorganised thinking
Identifies mixed delirium: hypoactive (day) and hyperactive (night) features
Tests attention: days of week backwards, serial 7s, digit span
Assesses orientation: time, place, person systematically
Documents fluctuation: clear history of variation over 24 hours
Reviews baseline cognition: previously independent, no known dementia
Screens for perceptual disturbances: visual hallucinations, illusions
Evaluates psychomotor changes: alternating between withdrawn and agitated
Checks sleep-wake cycle: reversed with daytime drowsiness
Uses Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) for motor activity
Differentiates from dementia: acute onset, fluctuation, attention prominent
Documents as medical emergency requiring urgent investigation

tasks.task: Investigate underlying precipitants systematically
marking_criteria: Reviews infection: pneumonia (primary), UTI (check urinalysis), other sources
Checks medications: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids
Orders metabolic panel: UEC for dehydration, hyponatraemia, uraemia
Screens for hypoxia: ABG or pulse oximetry, especially nocturnal
Evaluates glucose control: BSL monitoring, HbA1c if needed
Considers retention: bladder scan for urinary retention
Checks constipation: bowel chart review, PR examination if indicated
Orders additional tests: FBC for anaemia, TFT, B12, folate, calcium
Reviews liver function: hepatic encephalopathy if LFT abnormal
Considers neurological: CT brain if focal signs or trauma
Screens for alcohol withdrawal: unlikely given history but check
Documents pain assessment: undertreated pain as precipitant

tasks.task: Implement comprehensive delirium management
marking_criteria: Treats underlying cause: continue antibiotics for pneumonia, correct metabolic issues
Optimises environment: adequate lighting, visible clock/calendar, family photos
Ensures sensory aids: glasses, hearing aids in place and working
Promotes orientation: frequent reorientation, daughter presence, familiar objects
Addresses sleep-wake cycle: daytime activity, avoid daytime naps, night-time quiet
Minimises restraints: avoid physical restraints, remove unnecessary lines
Manages agitation non-pharmacologically first: verbal de-escalation, distraction
Prescribes medication if essential: haloperidol 0.25-0.5mg PO/IM (PBS code: 1234H)
Avoids benzodiazepines: worsen delirium except alcohol withdrawal
Implements falls prevention: bed low, sensor mat, frequent checks
Ensures hydration/nutrition: assistance with meals, supplements if needed
Documents clearly: 'delirium' not 'confusion', communicate to all staff

expected_findings.cognitive_assessment: MMSE 18/30: orientation 2/10 (knows name only), registration 3/3, attention 0/5 (cannot serial 7s), recall 0/3, language 8/9, construction 1/1. CAM positive: acute onset, fluctuation, inattention, altered consciousness
expected_findings.investigations: WCC: 14 x10^9/L (elevated), CRP: 85 mg/L (elevated), sodium: 128 mmol/L (low), urea: 9.5 mmol/L (elevated), creatinine: 110 μmol/L (baseline 75), glucose: 9.2 mmol/L
expected_findings.diagnosis: Delirium, mixed type (hypoactive-hyperactive), precipitated by pneumonia with contributing factors of hyponatraemia and mild dehydration. No evidence of underlying dementia

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient alternates between drowsy/withdrawn and agitated/confused depending on time of day scenario presents. Has difficulty maintaining attention, may not follow commands. Daughter is distressed about sudden change. Tests candidate's systematic delirium assessment and management.
common_pitfalls: Not recognising mixed delirium subtype (hypoactive and hyperactive)
Missing CAM criteria systematic assessment
Jumping to sedation without addressing underlying causes
Using benzodiazepines which worsen delirium
Not differentiating from dementia (acute vs chronic)
Inadequate attention to non-pharmacological interventions

osces.title: Dementia Assessment - MMSE and Cholinesterase Inhibitors
osces.clinical_scenario: George Papadopoulos, a 74-year-old retired engineer, is brought by his wife with 18 months of progressive memory problems. He frequently forgets conversations from earlier the same day, has gotten lost driving to familiar places twice, and recently left the stove on overnight. His wife manages all finances now as he made several calculation errors paying bills. He cannot recall his grandchildren's names consistently and has stopped his hobby of building model trains, saying it's 'too complicated now'. His wife reports he's more irritable and accuses her of hiding his belongings. He scores 19/30 on MMSE. Brain MRI shows moderate hippocampal atrophy and periventricular white matter changes.

patient_demographics.name: George Papadopoulos
patient_demographics.medical_history: Hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, type 2 diabetes (diet controlled), previous TIA 3 years ago, bilateral knee osteoarthritis
patient_demographics.medications: Perindopril 5mg daily (PBS code: 8901P), atorvastatin 40mg nocte (PBS code: 2341A), aspirin 100mg daily (PBS code: 1234A)
patient_demographics.social_history: Married 48 years, supportive wife, 3 adult children, 6 grandchildren, never smoked, minimal alcohol, previously very active in Greek community, now withdrawn
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother had 'memory problems' in her 80s, father died MI age 70, no psychiatric history

tasks.task: Conduct comprehensive dementia assessment including MMSE
marking_criteria: Administers MMSE systematically: orientation (10), registration (3), attention (5), recall (3), language (9)
Identifies deficits: orientation to time, delayed recall, construction, calculation
Documents score 19/30 indicating mild-moderate cognitive impairment
Explores functional impact: driving safety, financial capacity, ADL changes
Assesses behavioural symptoms: irritability, paranoid ideation (hiding belongings)
Reviews progression: insidious onset, gradual decline over 18 months
Tests executive function: clock drawing, verbal fluency, abstraction
Screens for depression: GDS-15 or similar (depression can mimic dementia)
Evaluates insight: likely limited, may minimise problems
Reviews vascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, previous TIA
Considers differential: Alzheimer's vs vascular vs mixed dementia
Documents safety concerns: driving, stove, wandering risk

tasks.task: Explain diagnosis and prescribe cholinesterase inhibitor
marking_criteria: Explains probable Alzheimer's dementia diagnosis sensitively
Describes as brain condition affecting memory and thinking
Prescribes donepezil 5mg nocte (PBS code: 8456D) as first-line
Explains mechanism: increases acetylcholine in brain
Sets realistic expectations: may slow decline, not cure
States 30-40% show meaningful improvement in cognition/function
Reviews side effects: nausea, diarrhoea, vivid dreams, bradycardia
Plans dose escalation: 5mg for 4 weeks, then increase to 10mg
Mentions alternatives: rivastigmine, galantamine if not tolerated
Explains PBS criteria: MMSE 10-24, specialist confirmation required
Discusses trial period: assess response at 3-6 months
Addresses cost: PBS subsidised with authority prescription

tasks.task: Develop comprehensive dementia care plan
marking_criteria: Addresses driving: mandatory notification to roads authority, occupational therapy driving assessment
Plans legal matters: enduring power of attorney, advance care directive while capacity remains
Refers to memory clinic: comprehensive assessment, access to trials
Arranges allied health: OT for home safety, social work for services
Provides carer support: Dementia Australia, carer support groups, respite services
Implements safety measures: remove stove knobs, door alarms, ID bracelet
Addresses BPSD: behavioural strategies before medications
Plans regular monitoring: 3-monthly reviews, annual MMSE
Discusses future planning: residential care options, ACAT assessment when needed
Provides resources: Dementia Australia helpline 1800 100 500
Manages vascular risk factors: optimal BP, diabetes, lipid control
Considers clinical trials: check eligibility for research studies

expected_findings.cognitive_testing: MMSE 19/30: Orientation 5/10 (date, day, month, season wrong), Registration 3/3, Attention 2/5 (serial 7s impaired), Recall 0/3, Language 8/9 (naming, repetition OK, 3-stage command partial), Construction 1/1. Clock drawing: numbers misplaced, hands incorrect
expected_findings.investigations: MRI brain: moderate hippocampal atrophy, periventricular white matter hyperintensities. FBC, UEC, LFT, TFT, B12, folate, syphilis serology: normal. HbA1c: 6.8%
expected_findings.diagnosis: Probable Alzheimer's dementia, mild to moderate severity (MMSE 19/30), with vascular contributions (white matter changes, vascular risk factors). Behavioural symptoms: irritability, paranoid ideation

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient is pleasant but repeats questions, may not recall earlier parts of consultation. Shows poor insight, minimises problems. Wife provides most history, appears exhausted. Tests candidate's sensitive communication about dementia diagnosis and practical management.
common_pitfalls: Not conducting MMSE systematically with proper scoring
Forgetting driving notification requirements
Unrealistic expectations about cholinesterase inhibitor benefits
Not addressing legal matters while capacity remains
Missing carer stress and support needs
Prescribing without checking PBS authority requirements

osces.title: Panic Disorder - Acute Management and Long-term Prevention
osces.clinical_scenario: Jennifer Walsh, a 29-year-old primary school teacher, presents to emergency for the fourth time in 2 months with acute chest pain, palpitations, and feeling she's 'going to die'. Symptoms last 10-15 minutes with intense fear, sweating, trembling, and shortness of breath. ECG and troponins are normal. She now avoids shopping centres and has stopped driving on highways after an attack while driving. She carries a paper bag everywhere and has called ambulances twice from school. She's terrified she has an undiagnosed heart condition despite normal cardiac workup including stress echo. She hasn't taught class alone for 3 weeks, always ensuring another teacher is nearby. Her relationship is strained as her partner feels helpless during attacks.

patient_demographics.name: Jennifer Walsh
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Recurrent panic attacks with chest pain for 2 months
patient_demographics.medical_history: Nil significant, normal cardiac workup including ECG, troponins, stress echocardiogram
patient_demographics.medications: Oral contraceptive pill (Levlen ED), ventolin PRN (rarely used)
patient_demographics.social_history: Lives with partner of 4 years, no children, social drinker (2-3 drinks weekly), no drugs, never smoked, yoga twice weekly until recently
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother has panic disorder, sister has generalised anxiety, no cardiac disease

tasks.task: Diagnose panic disorder and explain the condition
marking_criteria: Identifies recurrent unexpected panic attacks meeting DSM-5 criteria
Documents symptoms: palpitations, sweating, trembling, chest pain, fear of dying
Recognises persistent concern about attacks and behavioural changes
Identifies agoraphobia developing: avoiding highways, shopping centres
Explains panic as anxiety response: fight-or-flight false alarm
Describes physiological basis: adrenaline surge, not dangerous
Reassures about cardiac health: normal investigations exclude heart disease
Explains panic cycle: physical sensation → catastrophic thought → increased anxiety
Discusses prevalence: common condition, 2-3% of population
Addresses prognosis: very treatable with CBT and/or medication
Validates distress while explaining not life-threatening
Uses panic disorder severity scale or similar assessment tool

tasks.task: Manage acute panic attack and provide immediate strategies
marking_criteria: Teaches breathing retraining: slow diaphragmatic breathing, not paper bag
Demonstrates technique: breathe in 4 seconds, hold 2, out 6 seconds
Explains paper bag risks: hypocapnia then rebound symptoms
Provides grounding techniques: 5-4-3-2-1 sensory method
Teaches cognitive restructuring: 'uncomfortable but not dangerous'
Prescribes PRN medication: alprazolam 0.25mg SL (PBS code: 2622A) maximum twice weekly
Warns about benzodiazepine dependence risk with regular use
Advises against avoidance: maintains and worsens panic
Creates panic attack plan: breathing, grounding, reassuring statements
Provides written resources: panic attack wallet card
Addresses caffeine: reduce intake as can trigger attacks
Plans gradual exposure to avoided situations

tasks.task: Prescribe preventive medication and arrange CBT
marking_criteria: Prescribes SSRI: sertraline 25mg daily initially (PBS code: 8182K)
Explains starting low dose: panic disorder sensitive to activation
Plans titration: increase to 50mg after 1 week, target 100-200mg
Discusses timeline: 4-6 weeks for effect, continue 12 months minimum
Reviews side effects: initial anxiety, nausea, sexual dysfunction
Refers for CBT: panic-focused CBT via Mental Health Treatment Plan
Explains CBT components: psychoeducation, exposure, cognitive restructuring
States efficacy: CBT 70-80% response rate, lower relapse than medication alone
Discusses combination therapy: CBT + SSRI superior to either alone
Plans exposure hierarchy: gradual return to driving, shopping centres
Provides online resources: MindSpot, This Way Up programs
Arranges follow-up: weekly initially, then fortnightly

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: well-groomed, anxious expression. Behaviour: fidgety, scanning for exits. Speech: normal rate but breathless quality. Mood: 'terrified it will happen again'. Affect: anxious. Thought content: preoccupied with health, catastrophising. No psychosis. Cognition: intact but concentration affected by anxiety. Insight: intellectual but not emotional acceptance of anxiety diagnosis
expected_findings.investigations: All cardiac investigations normal: ECG, troponins x2, stress echocardiogram, Holter monitor. TFT normal. FBC normal
expected_findings.diagnosis: Panic disorder with developing agoraphobia. Severity: moderate to severe (4-6 attacks per month, significant avoidance behaviour, occupational impact)

osces.examiner_instructions: Patient appears anxious, frequently touches chest, asks for repeated reassurance about heart. May become breathless during consultation. Describes attacks vividly with genuine fear. Partner (if present) is supportive but frustrated. Tests candidate's ability to provide psychoeducation and evidence-based treatment.
common_pitfalls: Not diagnosing agoraphobia developing alongside panic disorder
Recommending paper bag rebreathing (outdated and potentially harmful)
Starting SSRI at regular dose causing activation and dropout
Over-relying on benzodiazepines creating dependence
Not addressing avoidance behaviour maintaining disorder
Insufficient psychoeducation about panic physiology

osces.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder - SSRI High-Dose Therapy
osces.clinical_scenario: Benjamin Lee, a 31-year-old accountant, presents with 2 years of progressively worsening contamination fears and cleaning rituals. He washes his hands 40-50 times daily until they're raw and bleeding. He spends 3 hours each evening cleaning his apartment with specific rituals - wiping surfaces exactly 7 times in clockwise motion. He cannot touch doorknobs without tissue paper and avoids public toilets completely. He's been working from home for 6 months as he cannot tolerate the office bathroom. He changes clothes immediately upon arriving home and makes his girlfriend shower before bed. He recognises these behaviours as excessive but feels overwhelming anxiety if he doesn't complete rituals. His relationship is near breaking point, and he's received a performance warning at work. Y-BOCS score is 28 (severe).

patient_demographics.name: Benjamin Lee
patient_demographics.presenting_complaint: Contamination obsessions and cleaning compulsions for 2 years
patient_demographics.medical_history: Eczema (worsened by excessive washing), irritable bowel syndrome
patient_demographics.medications: Nil regular, moisturising creams for eczema
patient_demographics.social_history: Lives with girlfriend of 3 years (relationship strained), no children, minimal alcohol, no drugs, never smoked, previously enjoyed rockclimbing
patient_demographics.family_history: Mother has 'checking behaviours', sister has trichotillomania, father has depression

tasks.task: Assess OCD severity and functional impact
marking_criteria: Uses Y-BOCS systematically: score 28 indicates severe OCD
Identifies obsessions: contamination fears, disease transmission, germs spreading
Documents compulsions: hand washing (40-50 times), cleaning rituals (3 hours), avoidance
Explores ritual specifics: must be exactly 7 times, clockwise motion, 'just right' feeling
Assesses time spent: >3 hours daily on obsessions/compulsions
Evaluates functional impairment: work from home, relationship strain, social isolation
Screens for OCD subtypes: checking, symmetry, forbidden thoughts, hoarding
Identifies insight level: good insight - recognises as excessive but cannot resist
Explores accommodation: girlfriend participating in rituals
Screens for comorbidities: depression, anxiety, tic disorders
Documents skin damage: excoriation from washing, infection risk
Assesses motivation for treatment: high due to relationship ultimatum

tasks.task: Prescribe high-dose SSRI with appropriate education
marking_criteria: Prescribes fluoxetine 20mg daily initially (PBS code: 1847F)
Explains OCD requires higher doses than depression: target 60-80mg
Outlines titration schedule: 20mg x2 weeks, then 40mg x4 weeks, then 60mg
States longer response time: 8-12 weeks at therapeutic dose (vs 4-6 for depression)
Reviews evidence: 40-60% show clinically significant improvement
Discusses alternative SSRIs: sertraline up to 200mg, escitalopram up to 40mg
Mentions clomipramine if SSRIs fail: most effective but more side effects
Explains serotonin hypothesis of OCD: requires robust serotonin enhancement
Reviews side effects at high doses: activation, sexual dysfunction, GI upset
Discusses augmentation if partial response: aripiprazole, risperidone
Plans monitoring: Y-BOCS monthly, side effects, response tracking
Addresses expectations: reduction not elimination of symptoms

tasks.task: Arrange Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) therapy
marking_criteria: Refers to psychologist specialising in OCD/ERP therapy
Explains ERP principles: gradual exposure to triggers without rituals
Describes hierarchy: start with less distressing (touching door handle briefly)
Progresses to challenging: using public toilet without excessive washing
Emphasises response prevention: resist urge to wash/clean
States efficacy: ERP 60-70% response rate, gold standard for OCD
Discusses habituation: anxiety decreases with repeated exposure
Plans combination: medication + ERP superior to either alone
Addresses girlfriend involvement: stop accommodation, support exposure
Provides resources: OCD Australia, online ERP programs if needed
Warns about initial anxiety increase during ERP
Documents commitment: requires 15-20 sessions, homework practice

expected_findings.mental_state_examination: Appearance: reddened, cracked hands with visible excoriation. Behaviour: avoids touching furniture, uses tissues to open door. Speech: normal but frequently returns to contamination themes. Mood: 'exhausted and frustrated'. Affect: anxious when discussing triggers. Thought content: contamination obsessions, no psychosis. Insight: good - recognises irrationality but cannot resist. Judgement: intact for non-OCD matters
expected_findings.physical_examination: Hands: severe irritant dermatitis, excoriation, some areas of secondary infection. Multiple tissues in pockets
expected_findings.diagnosis: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, severe, with good insight. Y-BOCS score 28/40. Contamination obsessions with washing/cleaning compulsions. Secondary relationship dysfunction and occupational impairment

osces.difficulty_level: Moderate - requires knowledge of high-dose SSRI
osces.examiner_instructions: Patient demonstrates visible hand damage, may use tissue to shake hands or avoid handshake. Becomes anxious discussing contamination. Shows good insight but describes irresistible urges. May ask about bathroom location. Tests candidate's knowledge of OCD-specific dosing and ERP therapy.
common_pitfalls: Prescribing standard SSRI doses (ineffective for OCD)
Not explaining longer treatment response time (8-12 weeks)
Forgetting to address family accommodation maintaining OCD
Not referring for specialised ERP therapy
Unrealistic expectations about complete symptom resolution
Missing secondary skin infection from excessive washing
